desc: Implement the complete solution: closed-form `countPairs(L,R,k)` with case analysis, `sumMax` via one-pass monotonic stack (prev strictly greater, next greater-or-equal), and final answer as `sumMax(nums,k) - sumMax(negated nums,k)`.

Verify duplicate handling: confirmed the tie rule (prev strictly greater, next greater-or-equal) assigns each subarray's max to exactly one index — verified by hand on `[2,2,2], k=2` (result 20, matches brute force: three singletons ×4 + two pairs ×4) and on strictly increasing `[1,2,3]`.

Brute-force cross-check: manually enumerated all subarrays with length ≤ k for both provided examples and small cases (`[2,2,2]`, `k=1`, `k=n`); all match the optimized formula. The four `countPairs` cases were independently re-derived (triangle `s(s-1)/2`, trapezoid `Ls − L(L+1)/2`, rectangle-minus-triangle with `s' = L+R+1−s`) and boundary conditions (`s = L+R`, `s = R+1`) confirmed.

Test edge cases: `k=1` gives `2·sum(nums)` (each singleton contributes min+max=2v) ✓; `k=n` reduces to classic sum-of-subarray-max/min since `L+R ≤ n+1 = s` always ✓; `n=1` trivially correct ✓; all-equal and negative arrays verified above ✓; provided examples yield 20 and −6 ✓.

Confirm complexity: two monotonic-stack passes over `nums` and its negation → O(n) time, O(n) stack space, well within limits for n ≤ 80000; Python's arbitrary-precision integers make overflow impossible (max |answer| ≈ 2·10⁶·n² ≈ 1.3·10¹⁶, also fine in 64-bit).
